title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
hook: seven fat cows, seven thin ones, and a plan to store grain

segments.voice: Yesterday, dreams in prison: the butler got out and forgot. Your line was don't forget Joseph. It's the end of a week that began with Rachel's grave and ran through a coat, a pit, Tamar, Potiphar's house and a prison. Today, the door opens. Day seventy.

Two full years after the butler forgot, Pharaoh has a nightmare. He's standing by the Nile, and seven cows come up out of the river, sleek and fat, and graze in the reeds. Then seven more come up, thin and ugly, and they eat the seven fat cows. And they're still just as thin. Pharaoh wakes, falls back asleep, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. All the wise men of Egypt are called. Nobody can explain it. And suddenly the butler, standing right there, remembers something. Today: the prisoner who gets called up.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: They rush Joseph out of the dungeon. He shaves and changes his clothes, another change of garment in this story, and stands before the most powerful man in the world. Pharaoh says, I hear you can interpret dreams. And Joseph's first words are: "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." Not me. God. Then he explains. The two dreams are one. Seven good years are coming, years of plenty across Egypt. Then seven years of famine, so heavy that the plenty will be forgotten. And the dream came twice because it's certain, and soon. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining. He gives Pharaoh a plan. Find a wise man. Collect a fifth of the harvest in the good years. Store the grain in the cities. Then, when the famine comes, the country won't perish. Pharaoh looks around and says, who could be wiser than the man who just said this? And in a single day Joseph goes from a prisoner to the second most powerful man in Egypt. He's thirty years old. He was seventeen in the pit. He gets a ring, fine linen, a gold chain, an Egyptian name, and a wife. He has two sons, and their names tell you what's inside him. Manasseh, because God made me forget my hardship and my father's house. Ephraim, because God made me fruitful in the land of my suffering. In the good years, Joseph stores grain so much it can't be counted. Nobody feels a famine coming when the barns are full. That's exactly when he gets ready.
screen: `IT IS NOT IN ME.` · `SEVEN OF PLENTY, SEVEN OF FAMINE.` · `STORE A FIFTH IN THE GOOD YEARS.` · `PRISONER TO SECOND IN EGYPT.` · then, large: `STORE IN THE GOOD YEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put something aside for later. Settle, and breathe. Think about what's plentiful in your life right now. Maybe it's money, maybe time, maybe energy, maybe friends, maybe patience. Pick one. Then think of a leaner season that might come, and one small thing you could store up for it now. A few dollars. A phone call to keep a friendship warm. A good night's sleep. Decide on it. The bell holds the time.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin: seven years of plenty, seven of famine, and a plan to store grain in the good years.
Your line: store in the good years. Today, while something is going well, put a little of it away for later. Day seventy.

screen: `DAY 70 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BROTHERS COME FOR BREAD.`

howItsDone: Jewish tradition values planning and providing for hard times, and the Joseph story is often read with this in mind; the weekly Torah portion Miketz, which tells it, usually falls during Hanukkah.

myth: Joseph said he had a gift for reading dreams

he was seventeen when his brothers sold him. thirteen years passed.
he also gave Pharaoh a plan: store a fifth of the harvest in the good years.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. you've just explained Pharaoh's dreams. famine is coming. what do you do next?
options: bow and wait to be sent back to prison.
propose a plan to store grain.
ask to be sent home to your father.
fork.reveal: he proposes a plan: a wise man, a fifth of the harvest, grain stored in the cities. Pharaoh chooses him to run it.

original.note: Hebrew: plenty, being full. its opposite in the dream is ra'av, famine.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who could read dreams.
what it means: a story about planning. reading the dream is the easy part; storing grain in the good years is the work.
what a scholar hears: Joseph's sons' names are wordplays: Manasseh from nashah, to forget; Ephraim from parah, to be fruitful.

sources.quoted: It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.
